This guide walks you through building one FlexiTac-V2 sensor (32 × 12 taxels), connecting it to a 32 × 16 reading board , and streaming it live to a heatmap on your computer. This is the standard setup: the fabrication guide, the firmware and PyFlexiTac all default to it. Each step links to a detailed page. Starting from scratch Order, assemble and stream. Fabricating a FlexiTac-V2 sensor is mostly lamination: no soldering, and no special tools beyond scissors or a craft knife. Once you have done it once, a sensor takes under three minutes. The steps below follow the fabrication video ↗ . It's worth watching once before your first build.

Everything for one sensor: the top and bottom FPCs, adhesive lamination sheets, Velostat and polyimide tape. Item BOM # Notes Top FPC and bottom FPC 1 One of each per sensor Adhesive laminating sheets 4 Two pre-cut pieces, one per FPC Velostat / Linqstat 3 One piece that covers the electrode area Polyimide tape 2 For sealing the edges FFC extenders (16- and 32-pin) and flat cables 7–12 For connecting to the reading board in step 4 Assembled reading board 5–6 Flashed or not; you can flash it later See Order parts for the full bill of materials.

A FlexiTac sensor is five thin layers. Both FPCs turn their copper electrodes toward the Velostat in the middle: the top FPC's 12 columns face down and the bottom FPC's 32 rows face up. Wherever a row crosses a column there is a taxel, and pressing it squeezes the film between the two electrodes. 1 2 3 4 5 Laminating sheet holds the top FPC from behind. Top FPC : 12 column electrodes, copper side down. You see its back here, with the copper showing through. Velostat : the pressure-sensitive film, cut to cover the electrode area. Bottom FPC : 32 row electrodes, copper side up. Laminating sheet

Attach each FPC to a lamination sheet and align it Peel a pre-cut lamination sheet and attach the top FPC to it. Do the same with the bottom FPC on a second sheet. Align the corners exactly, as in the photos: the two layers must line up when you stack them in step 2. Peel the lamination sheet. Place the FPC, corners aligned. One laminated FPC layer. Stack the Velostat between the two layers Place the Velostat in the middle, between the two prepared layers, centered over the electrode area. Close the stack with the second layer. Once it's centered, the sensor stack already works. Center the Vel

Fully seat the gold fingers. Push each FPC end all the way into its connector, straight and not skewed. The Adafruit extenders are wider than the gold fingers, so push the fingers against one side of the opening as you insert them; the side keeps them square. A finger that's half-seated, skewed or off by one pin is the most common cause of dead, swapped or shorted rows . Mind the cable orientation. FFC contacts are on one side only. If a whole sensor reads nothing, check that each cable's contacts face the connector contacts at both ends. The Adafruit extenders need practice. They're compact b

Both FPCs' copper electrodes face the Velostat. The Velostat covers the whole electrode area. The two FPCs are aligned, with no visible wrinkles. Gold fingers and flat cables sit straight and all the way in.
Your sensor is wired to the reading board. Now stream the sensor .

The Arduino Nano on the reading board runs a small sketch that scans the sensor and streams frames over USB. Flash it once, then watch a bright spot follow your finger on a live heatmap. That's a working sensor.

Get the sketch Download PyFlexiTac's firmware sketch ↗ ( Download raw file on that page) and open it in the Arduino IDE ↗ . Let the IDE move it into a folder of the same name. It is already set up for the V2 sensor: 12 rows, 32 columns, 2,000,000 baud. Select the board and port Tools → Board → Arduino AVR Boards → Arduino Nano , then pick the serial port under Tools → Port . If the upload fails with not in sync , set Tools → Processor → ATmega328P (Old Bootloader) and try again. Upload Click Upload . You only need to do this once per board.

Install PyFlexiTac Its live heatmap shows what the sensor feels. It needs Python 3.11 or newer . Find the serial port It asks you to unplug the board and reports the port that disappeared, such as /dev/ttyUSB0 on Linux or /dev/tty.usbserial-* on macOS. Open the live heatmap Don't touch the sensor for the first second: PyFlexiTac runs a baseline calibration , measuring each taxel's resting level. Then press with a fingertip and drag it slowly across the pad. Working sensor The live heatmap follows the press, in real time. What a working sensor shows: No contact: the whole map is dark and steady

flexitac-stream prints the frame rate and signal statistics. It tells you whether the board, the firmware and the reader agree. On its first read, PyFlexiTac runs a baseline calibration : it collects 30 frames and stores each taxel's median as the baseline. If you press the sensor during it, that pressure becomes part of the "zero." Each frame is a FlexiTacFrame : Field Type Meaning seq int Count of frames this reader has returned. It's kept on the host, so it doesn't reveal frames that were lost or skipped. timestamp_s float Host time when PyFlexiTac finished parsing the frame ( time.time() ), not when the board sampled it. USB and buffering add latency and jitter. raw uint8[rows, cols] Values exactly as sent by the firmware normalized float32[rows, cols] Baseline-subtracted, thresholded and scaled to 0–1 Useful methods and options: sensor.read() returns the next complete frame from the receive buffer, in order. Each reading board is its own USB serial device. For a two-finger gripper, open one FlexiTacSensor per port (find each with flexitac-find-port ) and read them in parallel threads, or call read_latest() on each in your control loop. The streams aren't synchronized : each board scans on its own clock, and frames reach the host with their own USB delays. To combine them, pair frames by timestamp_s (nearest in time) and allow for jitter.

flexitac-flash puts the same sketch on the board as the Arduino IDE path, without opening the IDE, and can generate it for a custom sensor size. h: Match the reader to the firmware
x: The reader must use the same rows and columns as the firmware. If they don't match, the reader splits the byte stream in the wrong places and the heatmap comes out cut off or scrambled ( what each mismatch looks like ). If you're writing your own reader, for a robot middleware, a microcontroller or another language, here is the whole protocol. For every frame, the firmware sends a two-byte start marker, then selects each row through a 16-channel analog multiplexer, steps through each column with shift registers, and reads each crossing with the Nano's 10-bit ADC, scaled to one byte. Field Value Transport USB serial, 2,000,000 baud , 8N1 Start marker 2 bytes: 0xAA 0x55 Payload rows × cols bytes, unsigned 8-bit, row-major (row 0 first, columns 0…cols−1) Value ADC reading ÷ 4 (10-bit → 8-bit). These stay with the sensor, a connector or a cable. If you have a spare, swapping it in moves the fault with it.

h: Rows with gaps, dead rows or identical readings
x: Example Gold fingers that went into their extender at an angle. Each press lights up two patches in the same column instead of one. Typical signs: A press lights up rows with gaps between them , as in the video. Some rows never light up. Neighboring taxels show exactly the same reading. The usual cause is gold fingers or a flat cable that went into an FFC extender at an angle. The extender joins each gold finger to its own wire in the cable. A crooked finger can touch two contacts, which shorts two lines into one, or miss its contact. The 20-pin extender ↗ is wider than the sensor's 12 gold fi

h: Some rows or columns never respond
x: Run flexitac-stream --port <port> --per-row and press along a column. Then check: Gold fingers fully and squarely seated in each FFC extender, pushed against one side of the opening (see above ). With the USB unplugged, re-seat both ends and both cables. Cable orientation. A cable inserted with its contacts facing the wrong way gives a whole dead side. Velostat coverage. A dead band along one edge often means the film doesn't reach that edge. Lamination alignment. If the top and bottom FPCs were offset when you stacked them, edge crossings may not overlap. Expected dead rows: with 32_16_fast.i

A value that stays flat at either end of the range usually points to a connection problem , such as a disconnected or shorted line. With the USB unplugged, re-seat the connectors and inspect the gold fingers and cables for damage. If that doesn't help, the fault can also be on the board: re-flash the firmware, then try the sensor on another board to rule out the board and its Nano.

h: The signal saturates or barely changes
x: Saturates under light touch: the sensor may be pre-loaded by its mount, or the baseline was captured under load. Redo the baseline calibration at rest. Barely changes under firm pressure: check that the Velostat is present and centered, and that the polyimide seal isn't holding the layers apart. Make sure you're reading the right port, and not another device.
These come from the reading board's firmware, the USB connection or how the reader is set up. The sensor itself is usually fine.

Try another USB cable. Many mini-USB cables only carry power. If the Nano's LED lights up but no port appears, the cable is the most likely cause. Check the USB driver. Many Nano clones use a CH340 USB-serial chip. Recent Linux and macOS versions include a driver. On older systems, install the CH340 driver from the chip vendor. Look at the kernel log (Linux) while you plug the board in: On Linux, brltty can grab CH340 devices. It's accessibility software for braille displays. The port opens, but the reader never finds a start marker ( 0xAA 0x55 ) followed by a full frame. Re-flash. A board fresh from the factory, or one running another sketch, isn't sending FlexiTac frames. Check the baud rate. Both sides must use 2,000,000 unless you changed it on purpose. At the wrong rate, the bytes arrive garbled and no marker is ever found. Check the port. Make sure you're reading the reading board and not another serial device. flexitac-find-port tells you which one it is. Close other programs that might be reading the same port (serial monitor, a second script).

x: Frames arrive, but the picture is wrong. Redo the baseline calibration with nothing touching the sensor. If the sensor was pressed during the first ~30 frames, the baseline is wrong. Call sensor.calibrate() or restart the stream. Mounting changes the baseline. Bending or pre-loading the sensor onto a curved finger raises its resting values. Run the baseline calibration after mounting, not before. Expect small fluctuations. normalized hides readings below the threshold (default 25 counts above baseline). If you work with raw , apply your own threshold or temporal filter. The hardware repo's fast_32_16.py uses an exponential filter wit

With PyFlexiTac's default firmware (12 × 32 frames at 2,000,000 baud), expect around 100 fps or more. That's a reference, not a pass/fail threshold: your computer, USB and visualizer change it. Much lower rates usually come from a slow USB hub, a very busy host, or a visualizer that renders every frame. For live use, call read_latest() so rendering never falls behind.

h: How long do FPC and PCB orders take?
x: Usually 1–2 weeks from order to delivery for the FPCs and PCBs, depending on your location and shipping method. An assembled reading board takes about one week.
In the authors' experience, sensors stay consistent and can often be used for about a year without significant degradation. Some teams have collected thousands of demonstrations without breaking one.

h: What if a sensor is damaged or malfunctioning?
x: Order a few spare sensors up front. Replacing a damaged sensor with a new one typically doesn't noticeably affect performance, so sensors are consistent across instances.

A tactile demonstration records what the sensor feels, what the camera sees and what the gripper does, all at the same moments. There are two ways to collect one. Teleoperation Drive a robot arm and record from the robot itself. One sensor, on the moving jaw. UMI data Hold the gripper and do the task yourself, anywhere, no robot needed. A sensor on each finger. Needs its own firmware. Simulation A third source: generate visuo-tactile demonstrations in Isaac Sim, without physical hardware. New to robot learning? You hold a UMI ↗ -style gripper and do the task yourself, indoors or outdoors, with no robot. A GoPro on the gripper records vision, and a FlexiTac sensor on each soft finger records touch. The open setup is Touch in the Wild ↗ (NeurIPS 2025). Its authors used it to collect more than 2,700 demonstrations across 43 tasks in 12 environments. Touch in the Wild reads the boards with its own code, not PyFlexiTac: a ROS 2 node while recording, and serial readers when running a policy. Check every session before you record. Run flexitac-stream or the heatmap and press each sensor: every row and column should respond. A dead row can't be fixed in data you've already recorded. Mount on something slightly soft, such as a fin-ray finger, so contact spreads over several taxels. Keep the cable still at the connector. The simulation lets you work with touch without any hardware. Simulated pads give the same 12 × 32 taxel grid as a FlexiTac-V2 sensor, on the fingers of a robot in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. The current release is the FlexiTac tactile simulation in Isaac Sim , which this page shows you how to build and run. It uses the same bimanual plug–socket setup and the same pad layout as VT-Refine , the research on fine-tuning visuo-tactile policies in simulation, whose own code runs on the older Isaac Gym. The repository is an Isaac Lab tree with two additions: a tactile sensor for FlexiTac pads, and an ALOHA environment whose four fingers each carry a simulated pad. You need: a Linux x86_64 computer (Ubuntu 22.04 or newer) with an NVIDIA RTX GPU and a driver of version 580.65 or newer, plus git and uv ↗ . Isaac Sim, PyTorch and Isaac Lab take about 30 GB. The trajectory viewer opens a desktop window; the browser interface can run headless. No FlexiTac hardware is needed. Each finger has a pad with a 12 × 32 grid of taxels at 2 mm pitch, the same layout as a FlexiTac-V2 sensor. On every step, NVIDIA Warp ↗ measures how far each taxel has pushed into the object's mesh. That depth becomes a spring force, clamp(stiffness × depth, 0, max_force) , which is then divided by max_force so each reading lies between 0 and 1. The taxels sit 1.4 mm in front of the pad's face, so a reading starts just before the object touches it; lower normal_offset (or pass --normal_offset to either script) for smaller contact patches. VT-Refine ↗ (CoRL 2025) trains bimanual assembly policies in three stages, from real to sim and back to real. It first trains a diffusion policy on about 30 real demonstrations per task. Each demonstration records FlexiTac pads on all four fingers together with a camera point cloud, the representation from 3D-ViTac . Next it fine-tunes that policy in a simulated copy of the setup with large-scale, GPU-parallel reinforcement learning. Finally it moves the policy back to the real robot.
